title: Removing embedded primes from a finite module
statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and $M$ a finite $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. For a prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$, write $M_{\mathfrak p}$ for localization [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] and define $\operatorname{Supp}(M)=\{\mathfrak p:M_{\mathfrak p}\ne0\}$. An associated prime is a prime equal to $\operatorname{Ann}_R(m)$ for some $m\in M$; an embedded associated prime is an associated prime that is not minimal among the associated primes. Among submodules $K\subseteq M$ whose support is nowhere dense in $\operatorname{Supp}(M)$ there is a maximal one. For $M'=M/K$, one has $\operatorname{Supp}(M')=\operatorname{Supp}(M)$, $M'$ has no embedded associated primes, and for every $f\in R$ contained in all embedded associated primes of $M$ the localization map gives $M_f\cong M'_f$.

proof.text: For finite modules support is the closed zero locus of the annihilator. Every submodule is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite]. Prove in Lean that, in a Noetherian quasi-sober space, a closed subset is nowhere dense iff it avoids every generic point of an irreducible component: each component contains a nonempty open, and the generic points are dense. In the subspace Supp(M), closure of a point p consists precisely of support primes containing p. Thus its generic points are precisely the primes minimal over Ann(M). Associated primes lie in support by the annihilator criterion; [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-support-prime-associated] then identifies the minimal associated primes with those minimal support primes.

proof.text: Define K as the intersection, over primes p minimal over Ann(M), of the kernels of M to M_p, using [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. The kernel criterion says m belongs to K iff at each such p some scalar outside p kills m. Therefore K_p=0 for all minimal support primes, and Step 1 proves its support nowhere dense. Conversely a submodule L with nowhere dense support vanishes at every such p; applying the same kernel criterion to its elements proves L subseteq K. Hence K is greatest, in particular maximal.

proof.text: The exact-sequence support identity Supp(M)=Supp(K) union Supp(M/K) and Step 2 show that M/K retains every minimal support prime. Every support prime contains a minimal one, so specialization closure proves Supp(M/K)=Supp(M). If q=Ann(m-bar) is associated to M/K, lift m-bar to m. Since m is not in K, it survives at some minimal support prime p. For r in q, rm belongs to K, so some s outside p kills rm. If r were outside p then sr would be outside p and kill m, a contradiction. Thus q subseteq p. The quotient support inclusion puts q in Supp(M), and minimality forces q=p. Every associated prime of the quotient is therefore minimal.

source.place: Tag 02M6 proof, quotient support and absence of embedded primes

proof.text: For p in Supp(K), choose a prime q minimal over Ann(K) contained in p. By [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-support-prime-associated], q is associated to K; by [lem-weil-pbc-associated-prime-submodule], q is associated to M. It cannot be a minimal associated prime of M, since K vanishes at those primes by Step 2. Thus q is embedded. The hypothesis on f implies f belongs to q and hence to p. So Supp(K) is contained in V(f), giving K_f=0 by the localization support criterion. Localization of the surjective quotient map is surjective; its kernel is localized K and hence zero, proving bijectivity.
